title: Build it backwards

prereqs.why: A `std::string` is read, indexed and grown here, which is three of the four things strings are for.
The loop walks the string from its last character to its first.

statement:
Read one whole line of text — spaces included — and print it
backwards.

```
input:   hello world        output:  dlrow olleh
input:   abc                output:  cba
input:   a                  output:  a
```

An empty line reverses to an empty line: print just the newline.

### The point of the problem

**Reading a line, not a word.** `std::cin >> line` stops at the
first space, so `hello world` would read only `hello`. The whole
line, spaces and all, needs:

```cpp
std::string line{};
std::getline(std::cin, line);
```

`getline` reads up to the newline and does not keep it.

**Indexing and size.** `line[i]` is the character at position `i`,
counting from 0, and `line.size()` is how many there are. So the
last character is `line[line.size() - 1]`.

**Growing a string.** `result += c` appends one character to the end
of a string. Start from an empty one and append the characters of
`line` from its last to its first, and what you have built is the
answer.

Counting down is where this gets awkward, and the awkwardness is the
point — see the boundary cases below before writing the loop.

### Constraints

The line is at most 200 characters, and may contain any printable
characters including spaces. There is exactly one line of input.

### Boundary cases

- **An empty line.** `size()` is 0 and the loop must not run. This
  is where counting down bites: `line.size()` has an **unsigned**
  type, so `line.size() - 1` on an empty string is not -1 — it is
  the largest `std::size_t` there is, and `line[that]` reads far
  past the end. Write the loop as `i > 0` over `i - 1`, or use a
  signed index, and the problem disappears.
- **One character** reverses to itself.
- **Leading and trailing spaces** are part of the line and are
  reversed with everything else.
hints: Read the line with `std::getline(std::cin, line);`, not with `>>`. With `>>` anything after the first space is left behind.
Build a second string rather than trying to reverse in place. Start it empty and append characters from the end of the original with `result += line[...]`.

Be careful counting down. `line.size()` is unsigned, so on an empty line `size() - 1` is an enormous number rather than -1. Looping `for (std::size_t i = line.size(); i > 0; --i)` and using `line[i - 1]` avoids it.
